blocks.text: There is only one company that can legally pipe water into your street, and only one that prints the naira notes in your pocket. You cannot shop around. When a seller has no rival and no close substitute, the ordinary discipline of competition disappears — and price becomes something the seller decides rather than accepts.

blocks.title: Monopoly
blocks.text: A market structure in which a single firm is the sole supplier of a commodity that has no close substitute, and in which entry by new firms is blocked. The monopolist is a price maker: it chooses either the price or the quantity, but not both, because the market demand curve constrains it.

blocks.markdown: The word comes from the Greek *monos* (one) and *polein* (to sell). Because the monopolist **is** the industry, the market demand curve and the firm's demand curve are the same downward-sloping line. To sell more, the monopolist must lower price — and it must lower price on **all** units, not just the extra one. That is why marginal revenue falls faster than price and lies **below** the average revenue curve.

items: **One seller, many buyers** — the firm is the whole industry.
**No close substitute** for the product, so buyers cannot escape.
**Barriers to entry** keep potential rivals out.
**Price maker** — the firm sets price along a downward-sloping demand curve.
**Marginal revenue is below average revenue**, and can even become negative.
**Abnormal profit can persist in the long run** because entry is blocked.
**No advertising is strictly necessary**, since there is no rival to advertise against.
Equilibrium is still where **marginal cost equals marginal revenue**, but price is read off the demand curve and exceeds marginal cost.

blocks.markdown:
### Sources of monopoly power

- **Legal grant** — a patent, copyright or an Act of parliament. The Central Bank of Nigeria has the sole legal right to issue currency.
- **Natural monopoly** — where a single large network is cheaper than duplicating it, as with water pipes, electricity transmission and railways.
- **Ownership or control of a scarce raw material** or a strategic input.
- **Very large capital requirement**, which few firms can raise.
- **Superior technical knowledge or a trade secret**.
- **Amalgamation or takeover** of all competing firms.
- **Government ownership** of a public utility.

blocks.caption: A monopolist's schedule. Notice that marginal revenue (₦100, ₦80, ₦60, ₦40, ₦20) falls twice as fast as price, because each price cut applies to every unit sold

blocks.title: Finding the monopolist's equilibrium output and price
blocks.prompt: From the schedule above, determine the monopolist's profit-maximising output, the price it will charge and the profit it earns.

steps.text: Apply the rule MC = MR. Compare the two columns unit by unit: at 1 unit MR ₦100 against MC ₦60; at 2 units MR ₦80 against MC ₦50; at 3 units MR ₦60 against MC ₦60.
At the third unit marginal revenue exactly equals marginal cost at ₦60, so 3 units is the equilibrium output.
Read the price from the demand (average revenue) column at that output: ₦80 per unit.

Check the profit column. Total revenue ₦240 minus total cost ₦170 gives ₦70. Profit is also ₦70 at 2 units, but the fourth unit would reduce profit to ₦30, confirming that output beyond 3 units is unprofitable.
Note the tell-tale sign of monopoly: price ₦80 is well above marginal cost ₦60. Under perfect competition the two would be equal, so the monopolist restricts output and charges more.

blocks.answer: Equilibrium output 3 units, price ₦80, abnormal profit ₦70 — and price exceeds marginal cost

blocks.markdown:
### Price discrimination

**Price discrimination** means charging different prices for the same commodity in different markets, where the difference is not justified by any difference in cost. A doctor who charges a wealthy patient more than a poor one for the same consultation, or an airline that charges more for the same seat at short notice, is discriminating.

It is only possible when:

1. The seller has some **monopoly power** — a price taker cannot discriminate.
2. The markets can be **separated** so buyers in the cheap market cannot resell to the dear market.
3. The **elasticity of demand differs** between the markets. The higher price goes to the market with the more inelastic demand.
4. The cost of keeping the markets apart is **less than the extra revenue** gained.

rows: Large scale allows economies of scale, lowering average cost
Absence of rivalry breeds inefficiency and complacency
Lower costs may be passed on as lower prices
Output is restricted and price is set above marginal cost
Patent profits finance research and development
A protected firm has little incentive to improve quality
Avoids duplicating expensive networks such as pipes and cables
Consumers have no alternative if service is poor
Price discrimination can let poorer buyers be served cheaply
Consumer exploitation and wider income inequality
blocks.caption: A balanced evaluation — examiners award marks for both sides

items: **Anti-trust or competition legislation** to break up or prevent monopolies. Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission was established by the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act of 2018.
**Price control** — setting a maximum price the monopolist may charge.
**Taxation** of monopoly profit through a lump-sum or excess-profits tax.
**Public ownership** of the monopoly so that it is run in the public interest.
**Removing barriers to entry**, including deregulation and allowing imports to compete.
**Subsidising a rival firm** so that it can enter and survive.

blocks.title: Do not say the monopolist "charges any price it likes"
blocks.text: The monopolist controls price only along the market demand curve. If it sets the price too high, buyers simply purchase far less and profit falls. The correct expression is that a monopolist is a **price maker** who chooses the price–quantity combination that maximises profit, subject to demand.

points: A monopoly is a single seller of a product with no close substitute, protected by barriers to entry.
The monopolist faces the market demand curve, so marginal revenue lies below average revenue.
Monopoly power comes from legal grants, natural monopoly, control of raw materials, huge capital needs, secret know-how or amalgamation.
Equilibrium is where MC = MR, but price is read from the demand curve and exceeds marginal cost.
Abnormal profit can persist in the long run because entry is blocked.
Price discrimination requires monopoly power, separable markets and different elasticities of demand.
Monopoly can deliver economies of scale but tends to restrict output, raise price and reduce efficiency, which is why governments regulate it.
